title: Flume‐simulated storms rejuvenated high marsh climax vegetation without compromising sediment erosion resistance
content:
Our findings indicate that clay rich high marshes may be resilient to extreme storms and may even experience some benefits to biodiversity without erosion resistance being compromised. Recovery of vegetation communities and persistence of erosion resistance indicates that post-storm intervention is likely not necessary for high marsh areas before the subsequent growing season, but rather that management of storm resilient marshes depends on allowing space and time for marsh recovery prior to the subsequent storm season. Given the occurrence of salt marshes in vulnerable coastal zones globally, the focus on monitoring marsh recovery during the growing season after an extreme storm could be key for their long-term viability for incorporation into coastal protection strategies.


Abstract

The contribution of salt marshes to coastal protection depends on the presence of a stable, elevated bed and the persistence of vegetation. As extreme storms may cause erosion and vegetation loss, long-term delivery of coastal protection depends on the system's ability to recover after disturbances and maintain its erosion resistance. We took clay rich high marsh substrate samples which had been variously damaged by extreme storm conditions generated in a wave flume. Samples were monitored for recovery and tested in a fast flow flume for erosion resistance. We observed rapid vegetation regrowth within 2 weeks after storm exposure in all samples (either clay rich or highly clay rich, as well as either root-rhizome mat intact or removed). Where dominant Elymus vegetation surface roots had been largely removed during the storm, more non-dominant species emerged during recovery. Since no erosion occurred below 5 cm in any storm-damaged sample, this indicates that (a) high elevation salt marshes may be able to recover rapidly from extreme storms and (b) where storm damage removes the surface roots, the storm may rejuvenate the climax vegetation community without compromising erosion resistance. Synthesis and applications. Our findings indicate that clay rich high marshes may be resilient to extreme storms and may even experience some benefits to biodiversity without erosion resistance being compromised. Recovery of vegetation communities and persistence of erosion resistance indicates that post-storm intervention is likely not necessary for high marsh areas before the subsequent growing season, but rather that management of storm resilient marshes depends on allowing space and time for marsh recovery prior to the subsequent storm season. Given the occurrence of salt marshes in vulnerable coastal zones globally, the focus on monitoring marsh recovery during the growing season after an extreme storm could be key for their long-term viability for incorporation into coastal protection strategies.
